pearls: Recruit the ultrasound lead sonographer.
Keep the audit to report text only; it is quick.
Pair with the incidental AAA referral audit.
Re-audit after 3 months to check the template holds.
effort: ~10 min per 10 reports from RIS
pass: The report gives a maximum anterior-posterior diameter and states it is inner-to-inner.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with intermittent claudication in vascular clinic are offered a supervised exercise programme?
why: Supervised exercise is first-line treatment but access is uneven. Vascular audits in the library focus on drugs and smoking [2038][2465]; none has audited exercise programme referral.

standard.wording: Offer a supervised exercise programme to all people with intermittent claudication.

population: Adults seen in vascular clinic with a new diagnosis of intermittent claudication. Exclude chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
sample: 40 consecutive new patients over the last 4 months.
data_source: Vascular clinic letters; exercise programme referral log; ABPI results.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add 'Supervised exercise programme: referred / declined / unsuitable (reason)' to the vascular new-patient clinic template, with a one-click referral.
reaudit: Next 40 new claudicants, same template.
close_loop: Present at the vascular network governance meeting. If it works, keep the template and report uptake to commissioners.
evidence: [2038] Vascular secondary prevention: smoking cessation advice 19% → 100% after a template
[2465] PAD inpatient risk factor optimisation: smoking cessation 40.5%, antiplatelet 38.9%
[2303] PAD best medical therapy: 4 of 11 smokers given cessation advice
pitfalls: No programme exists locally → audit anyway; the result supports a business case.
Advice to 'walk more' is counted as a pass → define supervised programme before cycle 1.
Patients seen at spoke sites are missed → include all clinic sites.
Attendance is low even with referral → measure it as a secondary outcome.
pearls: Recruit the vascular physiotherapist who runs the class.
Record distance to the nearest programme.
Use the audit to support a virtual or community option.
Share with GP leads to build referral routes.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass: The clinic letter records a referral to a supervised exercise programme, or that it was offered and declined, or a documented reason it is unsuitable.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults having major abdominal surgery lasting longer than the half-life of the prophylactic antibiotic receive a timely repeat dose?
why: Missed redosing in long operations raises surgical site infection risk. Antibiotic prophylaxis audits check choice and first-dose timing [2887][2272]; none has measured intraoperative redosing.

standard.wording: Before giving antibiotic prophylaxis, take into account the timing and pharmacokinetics (for example, the serum half-life) and necessary infusion time of the antibiotic. Give a repeat dose of antibiotic prophylaxis when the operation is longer than the half-life of the antibiotic given.

population: Adults having elective or emergency major abdominal surgery (colorectal, upper GI, HPB, laparotomy) where knife-to-skin to closure exceeded the local redosing interval.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible cases over the last 3 months.
data_source: Theatre system for operation times; anaesthetic chart or e-record for antibiotic doses and times; local antibiotic guideline for intervals.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Also triggers redosing in many guidelines

change: Add a 'Redose antibiotic due at __:__' line to the WHO checklist time-out, completed by the anaesthetist, with the time shown on the theatre whiteboard.
reaudit: Next 40 eligible cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the theatre users group and antimicrobial stewardship committee. If it works, keep the checklist line and whiteboard prompt.
evidence: [2887] Surgical prophylaxis: correct choice 50.4%, timing 58.5%; improved after multidisciplinary process integration
[2272] Lap chole prophylaxis: correct 24.4% → 55%
[2883] Ventral hernia prophylaxis: compliance 27.1% → 80% after local guideline work
pitfalls: Paper anaesthetic charts are hard to read → pilot 5 charts first.
Guideline intervals differ between antibiotics → list them in the template.
Anaesthetists may see it as surgical audit → co-lead with an anaesthetic trainee.
Long cases are few → include all specialties using abdominal surgery lists.
pearls: Recruit an anaesthetic trainee as co-lead.
Use the whiteboard time as a visible cue.
Report SSI rates from surveillance alongside.
Get the theatre manager to add the line to the checklist.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from anaesthetic records
pass: A repeat dose is recorded on the anaesthetic chart within 30 minutes of the redosing interval in the local guideline (for example 4 hours for cefuroxime or co-amoxiclav).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults on the general surgical wards who are able to take oral medicines receive paracetamol orally rather than intravenously on the day after surgery?
why: IV paracetamol is costly and is often continued after patients start eating and drinking. No audit of IV-to-oral paracetamol after surgery exists in the library.

standard.wording: Do not offer intravenous paracetamol unless the person cannot take oral medicine.

population: Adults on general surgical wards on postoperative day 1 who are documented as tolerating oral fluids. Exclude patients nil by mouth for a stated clinical reason.
sample: 40 consecutive postoperative patients over 2 weeks (point prevalence on ward rounds is acceptable).
data_source: EPMA administration records; nursing fluid charts; ward round notes for oral intake status.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Change the postoperative EPMA order set so oral paracetamol is the default and IV paracetamol needs a reason with a 24-hour auto-stop.
reaudit: Next 40 postoperative patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical audit meeting and drugs and therapeutics committee. If it works, keep the order set and share the cost saving.
evidence: [3054] IV metronidazole despite oral suitability 81.4% → 34.2% after education
[2232] Oral metronidazole use 12.5% → 61% in an acute surgical unit
[1529] Electronic prescribing order set: analgesia protocol compliance 0% → 58%
pitfalls: Oral intake status is poorly recorded → use the fluid chart and ward round note together.
Anaesthetists prescribe IV paracetamol in recovery → involve them in the order set change.
Nausea is used as a blanket reason → accept only documented vomiting.
Gains fade after the pharmacist leaves → rely on the order set, not reminders.
pearls: Recruit the surgical ward pharmacist.
Show the cost difference per day.
Collect data on two ward rounds a week for speed.
Pair with oral ibuprofen for a single analgesia message.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from EPMA
pass: On postoperative day 1, every paracetamol dose given is oral (or rectal) in a patient documented as able to take oral fluids or medicines.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults after elective abdominal or hernia surgery are prescribed regular oral ibuprofen for the first 24 hours unless contraindicated?
why: Multimodal analgesia reduces opioid use, yet NSAIDs are often left off without a reason. Postoperative analgesia audits in the library are mainly orthopaedic [1529][1321]; none has audited NSAID prescribing after general surgery against NG180.

standard.wording: Offer oral ibuprofen to manage immediate postoperative pain of all severities (including pain after dental surgery) unless the person has had surgery for hip fracture (see the recommendations on analgesia in the NICE guideline on hip fracture).

population: Adults having elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, hernia repair or other elective abdominal surgery. Exclude hip fracture surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive elective cases over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Theatre system for the case list; EPMA for postoperative prescriptions; pre-operative assessment notes for contraindications.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add regular oral ibuprofen to the elective general surgery postoperative order set, with a contraindication checklist that removes it when ticked.
reaudit: Next 40 elective cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical and anaesthetic audit meeting. If it works, keep the order set and report opioid use as a balancing measure.
evidence: [1529] Enhanced recovery order set: compliance 0% → 58%, ibuprofen 58%
[1321] Arthroplasty analgesia: protocol standard 34% → 61%, 87% of adherent cases used the powerplan
[2043] Analgesic ladder compliance 83.3% → 50.9% after teaching only
pitfalls: Surgeons worry about anastomotic leak → agree colorectal exceptions before cycle 1.
Renal function is not checked → build eGFR into the checklist.
Day-case patients are prescribed on discharge only → count TTO prescriptions too.
Opioid use goes up if NSAIDs are missed → record opioid doses as a balance.
pearls: Recruit a pain team nurse.
Use EPMA reports to pull data quickly.
Start with day-case lists, where the change is least contested.
Report AKI rates to reassure colleagues.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPMA
pass: Regular oral ibuprofen (or another oral NSAID) is prescribed for the first 24 hours after surgery, or a contraindication is documented (for example AKI, eGFR <30, active GI bleeding, NSAID allergy, surgeon request after anastomosis).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults referred on the suspected lower GI cancer pathway (excluding rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration) have a FIT result available at triage?
why: FIT at ≥10 µg Hb/g is now the gateway to the colorectal suspected cancer pathway. One unit went from 7 of 74 to 18 of 18 FIT use [2103]; a large trust found 103 cancers referred without FIT [2777]. No closed loop against the 2023 NICE wording is in the library.

standard.wording: 1.3.1 ... People with a rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration do not need to be offered FIT before referral is considered. [2023] 1.3.2 Refer adults using a suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal cancer if they have a FIT result of at least 10 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces. [2023]

population: Adults referred on the lower GI suspected cancer pathway. Exclude referrals for rectal mass, anal mass or anal ulceration.
sample: 50 consecutive referrals over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Cancer referral booking system; referral forms; pathology system for FIT result and date; triage notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Make a FIT result a required field on the electronic lower GI referral form, with referral returned to the GP with a FIT kit if blank (safety-netted for strong clinical concern).
reaudit: Next 50 referrals 3 months after the form change, same template.
close_loop: Present to the cancer alliance and colorectal MDT. If it works, keep the form rule and monitor monthly with the cancer services manager.
evidence: [2103] qFIT in 2WW referrals: 7/74 eligible → 18/18 after a closed loop
[2777] FIT-negative referrals: 103 of 1,037 cancers had no FIT
[3558] Memory clinic referral proforma: all blood tests 11.9% → 80% when proforma used
pitfalls: GPs object to returned referrals → agree the rule and safety-net with the primary care lead first.
FIT done after referral is counted as a pass → use 'available at triage' as the fixed time.
Patients who cannot return a sample are penalised → allow a documented exception.
Local form versions vary → check the form in use in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit the colorectal cancer pathway navigator.
Pull data weekly from the referral system.
Report conversion rates by FIT band to show value.
Share results with the cancer alliance, which may fund changes.
effort: ~10 min per 10 referrals from referral and pathology systems
pass: A quantitative FIT result is on the referral or in the pathology system at the time of straight-to-test triage.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults needing immediate emergency laparotomy have their pre-operative CT reported by a senior radiologist within one hour of the scan?
why: Delayed CT reports slow the path to theatre in peritonitis and ischaemia. Library audits cover time to CT [2612][2865] and CT discrepancies [2706], but none has audited report time and grade against the NELA standard.

standard.source: NELA Principal Standards (February 2025), CT scanning and reporting, citing RCS The High-Risk General Surgical Patient 2018
standard.wording: For patients requiring immediate surgery CT scanning should be undertaken immediately. CT results should be reported by a senior radiologist (ST3 and above) within one hour of being undertaken, regardless of urgency of request.

population: Adults in NELA who had immediate surgery (RCS definitions: peritonitis, perforation, ischaemia, haemorrhage, strangulation, tender obstruction or sepsis) and a pre-operative CT.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible NELA cases over the last 6 months.
data_source: NELA data extract (Q2.7 CT time, report time, reporter grade); RIS for scan and report timestamps; outsourced reporting logs.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: A 'NELA urgent' flag on the CT request that sends the scan to the top of the reporting worklist and prompts a phone call to the surgical registrar.
reaudit: Next 40 eligible NELA cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint surgical–radiology meeting and NELA local governance. If it works, keep the flag and review monthly with the NELA lead.
evidence: [2612] NELA QI: time to CT 2 d 19 h → <4 h, 30-day mortality 11.1% → 2.4%
[2706] Emergency laparotomy CT discrepancy 27.2% → 5.8%; only 23% reported within 24 h in cycle 1
[2680] Acute abdomen pathway: imaging within timeframe 60% → 78%
pitfalls: NELA fields are incomplete → cross-check times on RIS.
Outsourced reports lack reporter grade → ask the provider for grade data.
Radiology feels blamed → co-present with a radiology trainee.
Night-time cases dominate breaches → report by time of day.
pearls: Recruit the NELA lead and a radiology registrar.
Use the NELA extract to find cases in minutes.
Include surgeon–radiologist discussion as a second measure.
Show time from report to theatre alongside.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from NELA extract and RIS
pass: CT report (preliminary or final) issued by a radiologist ST3 or above within 60 minutes of scan completion.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults having emergency laparotomy with suspected sepsis receive antibiotics within one hour of the first qualifying NEWS2 score?
why: Delayed antibiotics in surgical sepsis raise mortality. One pathway audit fell from 80% to 50% in septic patients despite changes [2680]. No closed-loop audit against the NELA 2025 antibiotic standard is in the library.

standard.source: NELA Principal Standards (February 2025), infection management, citing AoMRC 2022 and RCS HRGSP 2018
standard.wording: Patients with a suspected “surgical” source of infection and NEWS2 of 5+, or >=3 in any one variable, should receive antimicrobials within 1 hour of recorded NEWS2 abnormality.

population: Adults in NELA with suspected sepsis at arrival or at decision to operate. Patients with NEWS2 1–4 are recorded separately against the 3-hour standard.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible NELA cases over the last 6 months.
data_source: NELA extract (Q2.10, Q2.11); ED observations system for NEWS2 times; EPMA or ED drug chart for administration time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: A 'surgical sepsis' PGD allowing ED and SAU nurses to give first-dose antibiotics from the trust guideline once NEWS2 ≥5 with suspected abdominal source.
reaudit: Next 40 eligible NELA cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the NELA governance meeting and to ED/SAU nursing leads. If it works, keep the PGD and report monthly via NELA.
evidence: [2680] Acute abdomen pathway: antibiotics within 1 h for septic patients 80% → 50%
[1200] Open fracture antibiotics: mean time 271 → 233 min, STAT prescriptions 15.4% → 51.7%
[1328] Necrotising fasciitis: all confirmed cases had sepsis six within 1 h
pitfalls: Prescription time is used instead of administration time → use administration only.
NEWS2 is recorded late → use the first observations timestamp.
ED and surgery each think the other owns antibiotics → agree ownership in the pathway.
PGD approval takes time → start with a pre-printed stat prescription.
pearls: Recruit an ED sepsis nurse.
Record where the patient was at the trigger point.
Present individual delayed cases anonymously.
Use NELA data so cycle 2 needs no extra collection.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from NELA and ED records
pass: First antibiotic dose administered within 60 minutes of the first recorded NEWS2 ≥5 (or a single parameter scoring 3).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults having emergency laparotomy have a mortality risk score documented at the end of surgery?
why: The end-of-operation risk decides critical care admission, yet audits in the library measure only the pre-operative score [2427][2571][2061]. No audit of the postoperative risk reassessment is in the library.

standard.source: NELA Principal Standards (February 2025), risk assessment, citing RCS HRGSP 2018 p37
standard.wording: Patients should have their risk of in-hospital mortality reassessed and documented at the end of surgery, using risk prediction tools and clinical judgement. Patients with an end-of-operation risk of death of 5%+, by any measure, should be admitted directly to critical care.

population: Adults (≥18) included in NELA.
sample: 40 consecutive NELA cases over the last 3 months.
data_source: NELA extract (Q6.1 postoperative risk); operation note; anaesthetic chart; critical care admission log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add a mandatory 'End-of-surgery NELA risk: __%' field to the emergency laparotomy operation note template, completed at sign-out.
reaudit: Next 40 NELA cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at NELA governance and the emergency theatre meeting. If it works, keep the op note field and link it to the critical care referral.
evidence: [2541] NELA frailty: CFS recorded 0% → 92% after a proforma item
[2427] NELA score on CEPOD forms in about 21%; missing in up to 97% of files
[2553] High-risk patients admitted directly to critical care: 38 of 43
pitfalls: The score is entered in NELA later but not in notes → count only contemporaneous documentation.
Surgeons and anaesthetists each expect the other to do it → name the anaesthetist at sign-out.
Intraoperative data are missing → allow a documented clinical estimate.
Template fields become default values → spot-check against NELA calculations.
pearls: Recruit the NELA anaesthetic lead.
Add the NELA calculator link to the op note.
Report the proportion of ≥5% cases reaching critical care alongside.
Build it into the WHO sign-out question.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from NELA and notes
pass: A numerical mortality risk (NELA, P-POSSUM or similar) is written on the operation note, anaesthetic record or immediate postoperative plan.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults with bowel perforation or ischaemia managed without surgery who die in hospital receive direct input from the palliative care team?
why: NELA now audits patients who do not have a laparotomy (NoLap), and many of them die in hospital. No audit of palliative care input after a non-operative decision is in the library.

standard.source: NELA NoLap Standards of Care (from April 2024), end-of-life care, citing RCS Caring for Patients Nearing the End of Life
standard.wording: The surgeon should seek to discuss the patient’s case with relevant professionals to ascertain: • the appropriate treatment options at the end of life available to the patient • the patients’ wishes, preferences and beliefs to inform their best interests. A formal consultation with the palliative care team is particularly useful in this context.

population: Adults (≥18) with bowel perforation or ischaemia where surgery was indicated but not done, who died in hospital.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 12 months (expect 20–40 in a DGH).
data_source: NELA NoLap extract or ICD-10 case list; notes; palliative care team referral log; individualised end-of-life care plan.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: An automatic palliative care referral prompt in the NoLap proforma when the consultant records a non-operative decision.
reaudit: All eligible cases over the 6 months after the change, same template.
close_loop: Present at emergency surgery mortality and morbidity meeting and to the palliative care team. If it works, keep the prompt and report through NELA NoLap.
evidence: [1938] Hospital deaths with dementia: palliative care involved in 40%
[1872] Advance care planning: treatment escalation plan 41% → 75% after an intervention
[1807] NACEL round two: individualised end-of-life plan in 71% of deaths
pitfalls: Patients die within hours, before referral is possible → record time from decision to death and analyse short survivors separately.
Palliative teams are small out of hours → accept telephone advice documented in notes.
Case finding misses non-operated patients → use the NoLap ICD-10 algorithm and M&M lists.
Surgeons feel judged about the decision → keep the audit on care, not the decision.
pearls: Recruit a palliative care consultant as co-lead.
Use the NELA NoLap extract for case finding.
Include the end-of-life care plan as a second measure.
Share anonymised family feedback if available.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from notes
pass: A palliative care team member reviewed the patient in person (or by documented direct consultation) before death.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults with a CT-confirmed ureteric stone and ongoing pain, or a stone unlikely to pass, have surgical treatment (ureteroscopy or lithotripsy) within 48 hours of diagnosis?
why: Early definitive treatment reduces stents, repeat procedures and readmissions. Renal colic audits mostly measure CT timing and analgesia; only two report time to definitive treatment [2624][2495], and emergency stenting often replaces treatment.

standard.wording: Offer surgical treatment (including SWL) to adults with ureteric stones and renal colic within 48 hours of diagnosis or readmission, if: pain is ongoing and not tolerated or the stone is unlikely to pass.

pass: Ureteroscopy or shockwave lithotripsy started within 48 hours of the diagnostic CT (or of readmission). A stent or nephrostomy alone does not count, except in obstructed infected kidneys, which are excluded.
population: Adults (≥18) with a ureteric stone on CT KUB who meet either NG118 criterion (ongoing pain not tolerated, or stone unlikely to pass, e.g. ≥10 mm or failed trial). Exclude obstructed infected kidney needing urgent decompression, pregnancy, solitary renal stones and patients who decline surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible adults over the last 3 months (extend to 6 months in low-volume units).
data_source: Radiology system for CT date/time and stone size; urology admission list and EPR for indication; theatre and lithotripsy systems for procedure date/time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
If yes, clock starts at readmission

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Ring-fence a daily 'hot stone' slot (ureteroscopy list or lithotripsy session) that the urology registrar books directly from the morning trauma/take meeting.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible adults, same template and same clock start.
close_loop: Present at urology governance and to theatre management with the stent and readmission counts. If it works, make the hot slot permanent in the theatre template and report the 48-hour rate monthly.
evidence: [2624] acute ureteric stones: treatment within 48 hours 35% → 53% (hot primary ureteroscopy theatre)
[2495] renal colic benchmark: surgical intervention within 48 hours 70% → 100% (renal order-set and leaflet)
[2049] ureteric colic: teaching only; clinic within 4 weeks only 26.4% after the change (teaching alone fails)
pitfalls: Clock start is disputed (ED arrival, CT, urology review) → fix it as CT report time and keep it the same in both cycles.
Cases miscounted when a stent is the only procedure → record the first procedure separately and count stents as fails unless infection is present.
Small numbers per month in small units → extend the look-back rather than shortening the window.
Theatre managers resist ring-fenced time → show stent change episodes and readmissions avoided, not just the percentage.
Gains fade when the rota changes → put the hot slot in the theatre template, not in a consultant's goodwill.
pearls: Recruit the stone lead and the theatre manager before cycle 1.
Agree 'unlikely to pass' (e.g. ≥10 mm or failed 4-week trial) before collecting.
Log delay reasons; they show which resource to ask for.
Pair with the stent database to show downstream stent burden.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from radiology, EPR and theatre systems

question: What proportion of men catheterised for acute urinary retention are prescribed an alpha blocker before their trial without catheter?
why: Alpha blockers before catheter removal raise the chance of voiding successfully. One ED audit found tamsulosin started in only 36% of men with retention [2281]; no closed-loop audit of this step has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Offer an alpha blocker to men for managing acute urinary retention before removal of the catheter. [2010]

pass: Alpha blocker (e.g. tamsulosin 400 micrograms) prescribed from the day of catheterisation or before the trial without catheter, on the drug chart, discharge prescription or GP letter; or a contraindication documented. Men already taking an alpha blocker pass if it is continued.
population: Men (≥18) catheterised for first-episode acute urinary retention in ED or on the urology take. Exclude clot retention, postoperative retention, known neurogenic bladder and men listed directly for prostate surgery without a trial.
sample: 40 consecutive men over the last 3 months.
data_source: ED and urology EPR for catheterisation date; e-prescribing or drug chart and discharge letter for the alpha blocker; trial-without-catheter clinic list for the TWOC date.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build an 'acute urinary retention' order set in ED and urology e-prescribing that includes tamsulosin 400 micrograms once daily and books the trial without catheter.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive men, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint ED–urology meeting. If it works, keep the order set, add it to the ED retention pathway and include TWOC success rate in the urology dashboard.
evidence: [2281] ED acute retention pathway: tamsulosin started in 36%, DRE 18% (baseline, no re-audit)
[2538] day-case surgery: pre-populated discharge order set, correct medicines 25% → 83%
[2495] renal colic: order-set raised NSAID use 54.5% → 71.9%
pitfalls: ED doctors discharge before prescribing → put the order set in ED, not only on the ward.
Alpha blocker recorded only in the GP letter → accept the discharge prescription as evidence and check both.
Mixing postoperative retention into the sample lowers the rate → apply the exclusions from the start.
Clinic TWOC outcomes missing → record TWOC outcome but do not make it a pass criterion.
Order set ignored after rotation → make it the default pathway item and brief new ED starters.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and the urology nurse specialist who runs the TWOC clinic.
Pull cases from the TWOC clinic list; it captures most retention episodes.
Show TWOC success by alpha blocker status; it persuades sceptics.
Agree the dose and the start day before cycle 1.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPR and e-prescribing

question: What proportion of patients whose first TURBT shows high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer have a second TURBT within 6 weeks?
why: Re-resection finds residual and upstaged tumour in high-risk disease. TURBT quality has been audited [3061][2787], but no audit in the library measures whether and when the re-resection happens.

standard.wording: If the first TURBT shows high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, offer another TURBT as soon as possible and no later than 6 weeks after the first resection.

pass: Second TURBT performed ≤42 days after the first TURBT.
population: Adults with a first TURBT showing high-risk NMIBC (high grade/G3 pTa or pT1, with or without CIS). Exclude muscle-invasive disease, patients going straight to radical cystectomy, and patients who decline or are unfit (record these separately).
sample: All eligible patients over the last 12 months (expect 30–50 in a DGH).
data_source: Urology cancer MDT database and pathology for case list and risk group; theatre system for both TURBT dates; cancer tracker for delays.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the MDT outcome for high-risk NMIBC automatically list the re-TURBT with a 'must be done by' date (day 42) on the waiting list, tracked by the cancer tracker.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: all new high-risk NMIBC since the change (at least 3 months), same template.
close_loop: Present at the urology cancer MDT and cancer governance. If it works, keep the MDT listing rule and add the re-TURBT interval to the bladder cancer dashboard.
evidence: [2052] mitomycin after TURBT: theatre–pharmacy system change cut delay 7.66 → 4.24 hours
[3057] open surgeon-level reporting improved TURBT resection quality
[3061] detrusor muscle sampling 39% → 66% (separate base specimen pot and dedicated surgeons)
pitfalls: Pathology or MDT delay uses up most of the 6 weeks → record each step date so the bottleneck is visible.
Differences in 'high risk' definitions → use the NG2 risk table and state it in the method.
Small numbers → use a 12-month look-back and all sites of the Trust.
Surgeons object when a patient chose delay → record patient choice separately and report it.
Waiting-list validation removes the date → ask the cancer tracker to flag re-TURBTs weekly.
pearls: Recruit the bladder cancer lead and the MDT coordinator first.
Report median days and the 42-day rate together.
Link to theatre scheduling so re-TURBTs get protected slots.
Include residual tumour and upstaging rates to show why it matters.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from MDT database and theatre system

question: What proportion of men starting androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer are offered a supervised exercise programme?
why: Supervised resistance and aerobic exercise reduces fatigue and improves quality of life on ADT. Bone health on ADT has been audited [1349], but no audit in the library measures the exercise offer.

standard.source: NICE NG131 rec 1.4.19 (2019, updated 2021; rec from 2014)
standard.wording: Offer people who are starting or having androgen deprivation therapy supervised resistance and aerobic exercise at least twice a week for 12 weeks to reduce fatigue and improve quality of life. [2014]

pass: Clinic letter or nurse specialist record documents an offer of, or referral to, a supervised exercise programme within 3 months of the first ADT dose.
population: Men starting ADT (LHRH agonist/antagonist or orchidectomy) for prostate cancer. Exclude men on end-of-life care and men already in a supervised exercise programme.
sample: 40 consecutive men who started ADT in the last 6 months.
data_source: Uro-oncology clinic letters and CNS records; ADT start date from the prescribing record or first-injection record; exercise service referral log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'Supervised exercise programme offered: accepted / declined' line to the ADT start clinic template with a one-click referral to the local programme.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 men starting ADT, same template.
close_loop: Present at the urology cancer MDT and the cancer alliance living-with-cancer group. If it works, keep the template line and report uptake yearly.
evidence: [1349] ADT bone health: none referred for bone health assessment when ADT started (related topic)
[1444] fracture clinic: awareness only, referral 5/38 → 23/43 (partial gain)
[1195] bone health checklist in discharge: antiresorptive prescribing 66% → 86%
pitfalls: No local programme exists → map options (physiotherapy, Macmillan, leisure centre schemes) before cycle 1 and report the service gap if none.
ADT started by GPs or oncology is missed → take the case list from the injection record, not only urology clinics.
Offers made verbally are not written → the template line solves this; audit written evidence only.
Clinicians see it as optional → quote the 'Offer' wording and fatigue data.
pearls: Recruit the prostate CNS team; they deliver most ADT starts.
Agree what counts as 'supervised' with the local service.
Give men a leaflet with the referral; uptake rises.
Record acceptance to show real demand to commissioners.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of women seen for the first time in a continence clinic with urinary incontinence or overactive bladder have a completed bladder diary of at least 3 days?
why: A bladder diary guides diagnosis and treatment choice, and avoids repeat visits. LUTS pathway audits show large gaps after referral [2821]; no audit in the library measures bladder diary use.

standard.wording: Use bladder diaries in the initial assessment of women with urinary incontinence or overactive bladder. Encourage women to complete a minimum of 3 days of the diary covering variations in their usual activities, such as both working and leisure days. [2006]

pass: A bladder diary covering ≥3 days is recorded or scanned in the notes by the end of the first specialist appointment.
population: Women (≥18) at a first urology, urogynaecology or continence clinic appointment for urinary incontinence or OAB. Exclude catheterised women and follow-up appointments.
sample: 40 consecutive new women over the last 2 months.
data_source: Clinic letters and scanned notes; appointment system for the case list.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Have the booking system send a 3-day bladder diary with every new continence appointment letter, with instructions to bring it.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new women, same template.
close_loop: Present at the pelvic floor MDT. If it works, keep the automatic insert and measure repeat-visit rates.
evidence: [2821] benign LUTS after negative cancer referral: 59% had no documented advice, pathway or follow-up
[2667] post-tonsillectomy discharge: one-click inserts raised key advice 21% → 93%
[2027] TCI form change removed listing errors (6 → 0)
pitfalls: Diaries brought but not scanned → count a diary summarised in the letter as present.
Booking team cannot add inserts → ask for an electronic letter template change or a text link.
Different clinics use different diaries → agree one 3-day format.
Women forget to bring it → add a reminder in the pre-appointment text.
pearls: Recruit the continence nurse lead and outpatient booking manager.
Record whether a diary was sent; it separates system failure from patient factors.
Measure decisions made at first visit to show time saved.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of children having grommets for otitis media with effusion have a hearing test about 6 weeks after surgery?
why: The post-operative hearing test confirms the benefit and decides discharge or follow-up. The 2023 NICE guideline made this a clear step; no audit of it has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Perform a postoperative hearing test 6 weeks after surgery for OME, and: If the hearing loss has resolved, discharge and: advise parents and carers to seek a reassessment by the audiology service involved in their child's care if they are concerned about a possible recurrence of OME-related hearing loss at a later date or consider a 1-year follow up with a hearing test if there are concerns a potential recurrence of hearing loss could be missed or consider an individualised follow-up plan if the child has an increased risk of unrecognised OME with hearing loss (for example, children with a learning disability or craniofacial anomalies).

pass: Age-appropriate hearing test (pure tone or play audiometry, or visual reinforcement audiometry) documented 4–10 weeks after grommet insertion.
population: Children under 12 having grommets (with or without adenoidectomy) for OME. Exclude grommets for recurrent acute otitis media and children under a separate cochlear or craniofacial service.
sample: 40 consecutive children operated on 3–6 months ago.
data_source: Theatre system for case list and date; audiology system for test date and result; ENT clinic letters.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add 'Audiology at 6 weeks post-op' as a default item on the paediatric grommet listing form, so the audiology request is generated at listing.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 onwards: next 40 children operated after the change (allow 10 weeks after surgery), same template.
close_loop: Present at ENT and audiology joint governance. If it works, keep the default request and add the rate to the paediatric ENT dashboard.
evidence: [2021] vestibular schwannoma: formal audiology done in 96.4% where a pathway exists (related topic)
[2667] paediatric tonsillectomy: one-click discharge inserts raised key content 21% → 93%
[2538] pre-populated order set: correct discharge items 25% → 83%
pitfalls: Audiology capacity limits → agree slot numbers with audiology before the change.
Tests done in community audiology are invisible → check community records or letters.
Did-not-attend counted as failure → record DNA separately and report both rates.
Window disputes → fix 4–10 weeks before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric audiology lead early.
Book the test at listing, not at discharge.
Include follow-up plans (discharge, 1-year test) as a secondary measure.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from theatre and audiology systems

question: What proportion of children listed for grommets for otitis media with effusion had hearing reassessed at least 3 months after the first test showing hearing loss?
why: Many OME cases resolve within 3 months, so surgery before reassessment may be unnecessary. NICE updated this in 2023; no audit of grommet listing against it has been published in the library.

standard.wording: 1.3.1 In bilateral OME (in both ears) with hearing loss, reassess hearing after 3 months. Where the OME with hearing loss is unilateral (in one ear), consider reassessment of hearing after 3 months. ... 1.3.2 In children who are experiencing hearing difficulties that significantly affect day-to-day living, consider intervening earlier than the 3‑month reassessment ...

pass: Two hearing assessments ≥3 months apart before listing; or a documented reason for earlier intervention (significant day-to-day impact, or a condition such as Down syndrome or cleft palate).
population: Children under 12 listed for grommets for OME. Exclude grommets for recurrent acute otitis media.
sample: 40 consecutive children listed in the last 6 months.
data_source: Waiting list or theatre system; audiology system for test dates; ENT clinic letters for early-intervention reasons.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add two required fields to the grommet listing form: dates of both hearing tests, or an 'early intervention reason' box.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 children listed after the change, same template.
close_loop: Present at ENT governance. If it works, keep the listing fields and share the rate with commissioners.
evidence: [2027] OMFS TCI form change: incorrect listing forms 6 → 0
[2110] MRI IAM requests: 85.3% met criteria (criteria-based request audit)
[2531] flexible cystoscopy: only 37.9% met indication criteria; local criteria and pathway introduced
pitfalls: Clinicians dispute the rule for severe impact → the early-intervention box keeps judgement while making it visible.
Tests from community audiology missed → check referral letters for dates.
Unilateral cases counted as fails → report bilateral and unilateral separately.
Listing form changes need IT approval → start with a paper sticker if needed.
pearls: Agree with consultants which conditions justify early surgery before cycle 1.
Show how many children resolved while waiting; it supports the rule.
Recruit the waiting-list manager to enforce the fields.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from listing and audiology records

question: What proportion of people who have a PET-CT after radical chemoradiotherapy for head and neck cancer have it 3 to 6 months after treatment ends?
why: A scan too early gives false positives and unnecessary neck dissection; too late delays salvage. No audit of post-chemoradiotherapy PET-CT timing has been published in the library.

standard.wording: For people having an FDG PET-CT scan after chemoradiotherapy, perform the scan 3 to 6 months after chemoradiotherapy has finished. [2018]

pass: PET-CT date is 12–26 weeks after the last radiotherapy fraction.
population: Adults who completed radical chemoradiotherapy for upper aerodigestive tract squamous cell carcinoma and had a response PET-CT. Exclude palliative treatment.
sample: All eligible patients over the last 12 months (expect 30–50).
data_source: Oncology record for last fraction date; PACS/radiology system for PET-CT date; MDT record for outcome.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Have the oncology end-of-treatment summary generate the PET-CT request with a 'not before' date of 12 weeks and a 'not after' date of 26 weeks.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 onwards: next patients reaching 12 weeks after the change (extend if needed), same template.
close_loop: Present at the head and neck MDT and radiology. If it works, make the timed request standard in the end-of-treatment pathway.
evidence: [2439] OG cancer: mean wait for PET-CT 17 days (1–57), timing variation (related topic)
[1704] cauda equina: locally adapted SOP met the 4-hour scan target in all cycles
[2052] theatre–pharmacy system change halved mitomycin delay
pitfalls: PET capacity is regional → share the data with the PET provider early.
Scans booked early to 'catch' recurrence → quote the false-positive risk.
Small numbers → use a 12-month look-back across the network.
Last fraction date hard to find → take it from the radiotherapy system.
pearls: Recruit a head and neck oncologist and the MDT coordinator.
Report equivocal scans by timing; early scans often cause them.
Keep the same date rule in both cycles.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from oncology and PACS

question: What proportion of smokers newly diagnosed with head and neck cancer are offered referral to a stop-smoking service at diagnosis?
why: Continued smoking worsens treatment toxicity and survival. The only head and neck audit in the library measured smoking status in inpatients, not the offer of help [2037].

standard.wording: Offer help to people to stop smoking, in line with NICE's guideline on tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence. [2016]

pass: Referral to a stop-smoking service (or opt-out referral) documented within 2 weeks of the diagnosis appointment.
population: Adults newly diagnosed with upper aerodigestive tract cancer who currently smoke. Exclude patients on end-of-life care only.
sample: 40 consecutive new diagnoses who smoke, over the last 6 months.
data_source: Head and neck MDT database for case list; clinic letters and CNS holistic needs assessment for smoking status and referral; stop-smoking service referral log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an opt-out stop-smoking referral field to the CNS diagnosis/holistic needs template that emails the Trust stop-smoking service automatically.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new diagnoses who smoke, same template.
close_loop: Present at the head and neck MDT and tobacco dependency group. If it works, keep the opt-out field and report quit rates at treatment start.
evidence: [2037] head and neck inpatients: smoking status documented 27.3% → 48.7% (education and prompts)
[2371] emergency surgery: smoking status 83% → 96% and specialist involvement 31% → 64% (structured teaching)
[1336] trauma: cessation offer 45.5% → 30.0% after education only (education alone fails)
pitfalls: Status recorded at diagnosis but not updated → capture the status on the day of diagnosis.
Clinicians feel it adds distress at bad news → allow referral within 2 weeks via the CNS.
Stop-smoking service capacity → agree the referral route before cycle 1.
Former smokers counted as smokers → define 'current' as smoked in the last month.
pearls: Recruit the head and neck CNS team and the Trust tobacco dependency lead.
Opt-out wording lifts uptake more than asking.
Measure quit status at treatment start as an outcome.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT and CNS records

question: What proportion of people with newly diagnosed head and neck cancer have their need for enteral nutrition assessed and recorded before treatment starts?
why: Weight loss during head and neck treatment is common, and late tube placement causes admissions. No audit of pre-treatment nutrition planning has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Assess people's need for enteral nutrition at diagnosis, including prophylactic tube placement. The multidisciplinary team should take into account: performance status and social factors nutritional status (weight loss, high or low BMI, ability to meet estimated nutritional needs) tumour stage tumour site pre‑existing dysphagia impact of planned treatment (such as radiation treatment volume and dose‑fractionation, concomitant chemotherapy, and extent and site of surgery). [2016]

pass: MDT outcome or dietitian record documents a decision on enteral nutrition (prophylactic tube, reactive tube, or not needed) before the first treatment date.
population: Adults newly diagnosed with upper aerodigestive tract cancer planned for curative surgery or chemoradiotherapy. Exclude best supportive care.
sample: 40 consecutive new patients over the last 4 months.
data_source: Head and neck MDT database; dietetic records; oncology or theatre system for first treatment date; admission records for unplanned tube placement.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'Nutrition and tube plan' field to the head and neck MDT outcome form, completed by the MDT dietitian.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the head and neck MDT. If it works, keep the field and report unplanned tube insertions yearly.
evidence: [3041] PEG audit: 7 patients had no MDT discussion before gastrostomy (related topic)
[1929] emergency laparotomy: referral proforma and electronic order raised geriatric review 40% → 100%
[2116] electronic hand trauma proforma: uptake 95–100%, 11/15 items improved

Decision recorded only as 'dietitian to see' → define that as a fail.
Mixed OMFS and ENT pathways → include both and report by team.
Unplanned tube counts are small → report them descriptively.
pearls: Recruit the head and neck dietitian as co-lead.
Agree the three allowed decisions before cycle 1.
Record weight at diagnosis; it strengthens the case for the field.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from MDT and dietetic records

question: What proportion of people with early (T1–T2, N0) oral cavity cancer have sentinel lymph node biopsy rather than elective neck dissection?
why: Sentinel node biopsy stages the neck with less morbidity than elective neck dissection. No audit of neck management in early oral cancer has been published in the library; SLNB audits exist only for melanoma [2519][2354].

standard.wording: Offer sentinel lymph node biopsy instead of elective neck dissection to people with early oral cavity cancer (grade T1 to T2, N0), unless they need cervical access at the same time (for example, free‑flap reconstruction). [2016]

pass: SLNB performed; or elective neck dissection with documented need for cervical access (e.g. free-flap reconstruction).
population: Adults with new clinically T1–T2 N0 oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma treated with primary surgery. Exclude recurrent disease and patients not fit for neck surgery.
sample: All eligible patients over the last 24 months (expect 30–40 in a head and neck centre).
data_source: Head and neck MDT database for staging; operation notes and theatre system for procedure; pathology for nodal findings.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'SLNB' option to the MDT outcome form for cT1–2N0 oral cancer, with a required reason if elective neck dissection is chosen.
reaudit: Wk 13–14 onwards: all new eligible cases since the change (extend to 6 months), plus any retrospective catch-up, same template.
close_loop: Present at the head and neck MDT and network governance. If it works, keep the default and report SLNB rate and positive rate annually.
evidence: [2519] melanoma SLNB: compliance with NICE indications 91.4% → 92.6% (presentation only)
[2354] melanoma SLNB referrals: standard referral letters cut non-compliant cases 6.5% → 3%
[2027] listing form change removed errors (form fix works)

Small numbers → use 24 months and all network sites.
Surgeons prefer neck dissection → the reason box keeps choice visible and discussable.
Staging changes on pathology → classify by clinical stage at MDT.
pearls: Recruit the OMFS head and neck lead and nuclear medicine.
Report morbidity (shoulder, length of stay) alongside the rate.
Agree the cervical access exception wording first.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from MDT, op notes and pathology

question: What proportion of patients having surgical removal of impacted wisdom teeth have a NICE-listed indication documented before surgery?
why: Prophylactic removal of disease-free wisdom teeth adds risk without benefit. OMFS audits in the library cover antibiotics [2113] and wrong-tooth errors [2027], not the indication itself.

standard.wording: 1.1 The practice of prophylactic removal of pathology-free impacted third molars should be discontinued in the NHS. ... 1.3 Surgical removal of impacted third molars should be limited to patients with evidence of pathology. Such pathology includes unrestorable caries, non-treatable pulpal and/or periapical pathology, cellulitis, abscess and osteomyelitis, internal/external resorption of the tooth or adjacent teeth, fracture of tooth, disease of follicle including cyst/tumour, tooth/teeth impeding surgery or reconstructive jaw surgery, and when a tooth is involved in or within the field of tumour resection. 1.4 ... Second or subsequent episodes should be considered the appropriate indication for surgery.

pass: Clinic letter, listing form or consent names a TA1 indication (listed pathology, or two or more episodes of pericoronitis, or one particularly severe episode).
population: Adults having surgical removal of one or more impacted third molars (day case or local anaesthetic). Exclude removal as part of tumour or trauma surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: Theatre or clinic procedure list; clinic letters, TCI forms and consent forms; radiograph reports.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace free text on the wisdom tooth listing (TCI) form with a mandatory tick-box list of TA1 indications plus 'other (specify)'.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at OMFS governance. If it works, keep the form and audit 'other' reasons yearly.
evidence: [2027] OMFS: TCI form change after RCA, incorrect forms 6 → 0 and no wrong-tooth extractions
[2113] third molar surgery: only 9% had clear justification for antibiotics (documentation gap)
[2531] flexible cystoscopy: 37.9% met indications; local criteria introduced
pitfalls: Surgeons cite reasons outside TA1 (e.g. distal caries risk in the second molar) → record these as 'other' and discuss them rather than failing silently.
Indication in the referral but not the letter → accept any pre-operative OMFS document.
Mixed operators (dental core trainees, staff grades) → report by grade to target teaching.
The form becomes a tick-box habit → spot-check 10 notes against radiographs.
pearls: Recruit the OMFS clinical lead and the day-surgery booking team.
Agree how to classify 'other' reasons before cycle 1.
Include pericoronitis episode counts; they are the most common grey area.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from letters and TCI forms

question: What proportion of people newly diagnosed with melanoma have vitamin D measured at diagnosis in secondary care?
why: Low vitamin D is linked with worse melanoma outcomes, and sun-protection advice can lower it further. No audit of vitamin D testing in melanoma has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Measure vitamin D levels at diagnosis in secondary care in all people with melanoma. [2015]

pass: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D result dated within 3 months of the histological diagnosis.
population: Adults with a new diagnosis of invasive cutaneous melanoma (any stage). Exclude melanoma in situ and recurrent disease.
sample: 40 consecutive new melanomas over the last 4 months.
data_source: Skin cancer MDT database or pathology for case list and diagnosis date; pathology system for vitamin D result; clinic letters for supplementation advice.

change: Add vitamin D to the 'new melanoma' results-clinic order set used by the skin cancer CNS.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new melanomas, same template.
close_loop: Present at the skin cancer MDT. If it works, keep the order set and report supplementation advice as a second measure.
evidence: [1195] bone health: checklist, vitamin D measured in 93% and antiresorptive prescribing 66% → 86%

[2495] renal colic: order-set raised calcium testing 77.9% → 94.7%

question: What proportion of patients attending the emergency department with a burn that meets national referral thresholds are referred to a specialised burn service?
why: Under-referral delays specialist care and grafting; burn size is often not estimated. Burns audits in the library cover admission proforma quality in a burn unit [2032], not referral from the front door.

standard.source: National Network for Burn Care, National Burn Care Referral Guidance, section 3 (2012; hosted by the British Burn Association)
standard.wording: The suggested minimum threshold for referral into specialised burn care services can be summarised as: All burns ≥2% TBSA in children or ≥3% in adults All full thickness burns All circumferential burns Any burn not healed in 2 weeks Any burn with suspicion of non-accidental injury should be referred to a Burn Unit/Centre for expert assessment within 24 hours

pass: Referral to, or documented discussion with, a specialised burn service (facility, unit or centre) for a burn meeting any threshold, during the ED attendance or within 24 hours.
population: All ED attendances with a burn injury (thermal, scald, chemical, electrical) that meet at least one referral threshold. Include children (<16) and adults. Exclude sunburn.
sample: 40 consecutive qualifying attendances over the last 3 months.
data_source: ED EPR (diagnosis codes and free-text search) for case list and TBSA; burns network referral portal or telephone log for referral.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Introduce an ED burns proforma with a Lund and Browder chart and a 'refer if' box that links to the burns network referral portal.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 qualifying attendances, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED governance and the regional burns network meeting. If it works, keep the proforma in the ED system and audit yearly.
evidence: [2032] burns admission proforma: TBSA documented 83% → 93% (redesigned flowchart proforma)
[2083] facial lacerations: checklist sticker introduced after 58% had no tetanus assessment
[2364] lacerations: tetanus managed 59%, wound size 49% (free-text documentation gaps)

Referrals by phone leave no record → ask the burns service for its referral log.

Use the network's own referral portal data for cross-checking.
Measure Lund and Browder use; it drives correct TBSA.

question: What proportion of patients with a hand injury or burn seen by plastic surgery have tetanus prophylaxis managed in line with UKHSA guidance?
why: Tetanus-prone wounds need vaccine or immunoglobulin based on immunisation status. Laceration and open fracture audits show tetanus assessment missing in about half of cases [2364][2083][1274]; no plastic surgery audit exists in the library.

standard.source: UKHSA, Guidance on the management of suspected tetanus cases and the assessment and management of tetanus-prone wounds, sections 7.2–7.3 and Table 4 (updated July 2026)
standard.wording: If the wound, burn or injury fulfils the criteria for a high-risk tetanus-prone wound, intramuscular tetanus immunoglobulin (IM-TIG ) should be considered (see Table 4 and section 6). ... A reinforcing dose of tetanus-containing vaccine is recommended (see Table 4).

pass: Immunisation status and wound category (clean, tetanus-prone, high-risk tetanus-prone) documented, and vaccine and/or immunoglobulin given when Table 4 requires it.
population: Patients of any age seen by plastic surgery (hand trauma clinic, burns clinic or admission) with an open hand injury or a burn. Exclude closed injuries.
sample: 40 consecutive patients over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Hand trauma and burns clerking proformas; ED record; drug chart or ED administration record for vaccine or immunoglobulin; GP summary care record for status where needed.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Embed a three-step tetanus box (status → wound category → action from Table 4) in the hand trauma and burns clerking proformas.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at plastics and ED joint governance. If it works, keep the proforma box and share it with the ED minor injuries team.

[1274] open fractures: documented tetanus assessment 4.87%
[2116] electronic hand trauma proforma: uptake 95–100%, 11/15 items improved

Status unknown in adults → Table 4 treats uncertain status as not adequately primed; teach that rule.
Immunoglobulin supply → confirm the local HNIG/IM-TIG product and route first.
Guidance updates between cycles → use the same version for both cycles and note the date.
pearls: Recruit the hand trauma nurse lead and ED pharmacist.
Print Table 4 on the back of the proforma.
Use the GP summary care record to confirm status quickly.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from proformas and drug charts

question: What proportion of patients admitted with a human or animal bite on intravenous antibiotics are reviewed for a switch to oral antibiotics within 48 hours?

population: Patients of any age admitted under plastic or hand surgery with a human or animal bite who receive IV antibiotics. Exclude patients with sepsis requiring critical care.
sample: 40 consecutive admissions over the last 6 months.
data_source: Admission list and EPR; e-prescribing or drug chart for first IV dose and switch time; ward round notes for review.

change: Set the electronic anaesthetic record to prompt a temperature entry at induction and every 30 minutes (or link a continuous temperature probe to the monitor feed), with a 36.0°C alert.

evidence: [1712] Salford trauma theatres: temperature documented in 35% (single cycle; mandatory field planned)
[2325] Tertiary emergency general surgery: >18% hypothermic at knife-to-skin → 100% normothermic (forced-air warming from 45 minutes pre-op)
[1422] Glasgow Royal Infirmary: mean recovery temperature 35.5°C → 36.6°C (consistent warming changes)
pitfalls: Monitor records temperature but it is not exported to the chart → check that the data feed is on before cycle 1.
Tympanic infrared readings are indirect estimates (NICE 1.1.6) → record the site and report it separately.
Short cases with one reading distort results → apply the >30-minute rule in both cycles.
Staff see it as box-ticking → show the recovery hypothermia rate alongside compliance.
pearls: Recruit an ODP lead; ODPs usually place the probe.
Audit one theatre suite first if paper charts are mixed with electronic ones.
Record the lowest temperature too; it makes the case for warming equipment.

question: What proportion of adults sent from the ward or emergency department for surgery have a temperature recorded in the hour before they leave?
why: Hypothermia audits in the library start in theatre or recovery [1422] [1406] [2325]; the pre-transfer ward temperature that triggers pre-warming has not been measured in a closed loop.

standard.wording: The patient's temperature should be measured and documented in the hour before they leave the ward or emergency department. [2008]

pass: A temperature documented within 60 minutes before the time the patient left the ward or emergency department for theatre.
population: Adults (18+) transferred from a surgical ward, surgical admissions unit or ED to theatre for non-orthopaedic surgery. Exclude day-surgery patients who walk from a separate unit if that unit has its own pathway (audit separately).
sample: 40 consecutive patients over 2 weeks from two surgical wards and ED.
data_source: E-observations (temperature times); theatre system or ward transfer log (time sent for / time left ward); pre-op checklist.

change: Add 'Temperature in last hour ___°C (time ___); if <36.0°C start warming' as a mandatory field on the pre-operative transfer checklist.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: 40 consecutive patients, same areas and template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical nursing forum and theatre users' group. If it works, keep the field and add the result to the Sign In.
evidence: [2325] Tertiary emergency general surgery: >18% hypothermic at knife-to-skin → 100% normothermic (forced-air warming before theatre)
[1422] Glasgow Royal Infirmary: mean recovery temperature 35.5°C → 36.6°C (warming changes)
[3024] Large English trust colorectal surgery: pre-bundle audit found local ward practices to target (single cycle)

Ward nurses object to extra observations → the field replaces a free-text line on the existing checklist.
Emergency patients sent urgently → accept 'clinical urgency' documented as an exclusion.
Gains fade after rotation → make the field mandatory in the electronic checklist.
pearls: Recruit a ward sister and a theatre reception nurse.
Theatre reception can refuse to accept a checklist without the temperature during weeks 5–12.
Report how many patients were below 36.0°C; it shows why it matters.
Agree the time source before cycle 1.

question: What proportion of discharges from critical care to a general ward between 22:00 and 07:00 are reported as adverse incidents?
why: Out-of-hours ICU discharge is linked with readmission and death, and NICE asks that each one is reported. Library ICU transfer work covers discharge letters [77] and handover [2271], not night discharges or their reporting.

standard.wording: After the decision to transfer a patient from a critical care area to the general ward has been made, he or she should be transferred as early as possible during the day. Transfer from critical care areas to the general ward between 10:00pm and 7:00am should be avoided whenever possible, and should be documented as an adverse incident if it occurs.

pass: A ward transfer between 22:00 and 07:00 has a matching incident report (Datix or equivalent).
population: All adult discharges from ICU/HDU to a general ward. Exclude transfers to another critical care unit, theatre, or deaths.
sample: All ward discharges over the last 3 months (typically 150–250), with every 22:00–07:00 transfer (expect 10–40) checked for an incident report.
data_source: ICU admission/discharge system or ICNARC data (decision-to-discharge and actual discharge times); incident reporting system (search by date and unit).

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'Discharge time 22:00–07:00? Incident number ___' field to the ICU electronic discharge form, and a nightly report of such discharges to the nurse in charge.
target: ≥90% of night discharges reported; secondary: fall in night discharges
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: all ward discharges in the preceding 2 months, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU governance and the hospital bed management meeting. If it works, share monthly night-discharge counts on the ICU dashboard.
evidence: [77] UHBW ICU-to-ward transfers: poor discharge letters → discharge letter improved
[2271] Royal Papworth theatre-to-critical care handover: postoperative instructions 30% → 45%
pitfalls: Nurses feel blamed by incident reporting → frame reports as capacity data for the board, not individual error.
Decision time and actual time confused → record both; the standard is about actual transfer.
Small numbers → use all discharges over 3 months, not a sample.
Bed managers push back → invite them to the presentation and show readmission data.
pearls: ICNARC case mix data already hold discharge times; ask the ICNARC data clerk.
Recruit the ICU matron as co-lead.
Report time from decision to discharge; it shows the day-time delays that cause night moves.
Keep the report monthly after the audit.
effort: ~2 h total from ICNARC/ICU system and incident log

question: In adults admitted to critical care from a ward or the emergency department, what proportion have a documented admission decision involving both the referring consultant and the critical care consultant?
why: Consultant-to-consultant discussion improves decisions about escalation, but library ICU audits look at NEWS2 before admission [507] and frailty scoring [2790], not who made the admission decision.

standard.wording: If the team caring for the patient considers that admission to a critical care area is clinically indicated, then the decision to admit should involve both the consultant caring for the patient on the ward and the consultant in critical care.

pass: The ICU admission note or referral record names both the parent-team consultant and the critical care consultant as involved in the decision.
population: Unplanned adult admissions to ICU/HDU from wards or ED. Exclude planned post-operative admissions, direct theatre admissions and cardiac arrest admissions.
sample: 40 consecutive unplanned admissions over the last 2 months.
data_source: ICU admission clerking and referral proforma; parent-team notes; ICU admissions log.

close_loop: Present at ICU and medical/surgical governance. If it works, keep the fields and report out-of-hours compliance quarterly.
evidence: [78] UHBW emergency ICU admissions from wards: missed deterioration → trainee training and a new outreach team
[2790] Morriston ICU: Clinical Frailty Scale completion 52% → 68% (posters, handover reminders)

Parent consultants feel policed → present as shared decision-making support, with parent-team representation.
Referral through outreach blurs who spoke to whom → record the parent consultant contact explicitly.
Definitions drift → lock the exclusion list before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit an acute medicine consultant; most ward admissions are medical.
Check that the ICU admission proforma is the source of truth before cycle 1.
Report the proportion with a treatment escalation plan at the same time; it is often the real gap.
Name an ICU consultant sponsor.

question: In adults in critical care at risk of long-term problems, what proportion have rehabilitation goals agreed and documented within 4 days of admission or before critical care discharge, whichever is sooner?
why: NCEPOD's 2025 report 'Recovery beyond survival' found comprehensive rehabilitation assessments often missing. No closed-loop audit of rehabilitation goals after critical illness is in the library; the closest shows structured documentation doubled goal setting in a rehabilitation unit [1827].

standard.source: NICE QS158 statement 1 (2017), from NICE CG83 rec 1.4
standard.wording: Adults in critical care at risk of morbidity have their rehabilitation goals agreed within 4 days of admission to critical care or before discharge from critical care, whichever is sooner.

pass: Short-term and medium-term rehabilitation goals documented (by any member of the critical care MDT) by day 4 of admission, or before discharge if the stay was shorter.
population: Adults admitted to ICU/HDU who meet any 'at risk' criterion on a short clinical assessment (e.g. ventilated, stay expected >4 days, unable to get out of bed independently, premorbid mobility problems). Exclude deaths and end-of-life care within 4 days.
sample: 40 consecutive at-risk admissions over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ICU notes and physiotherapy/OT records (rehabilitation goals, dates); ICU admission system (admission and discharge dates).

change: Add a 'Rehabilitation goals (short-term / medium-term) – agreed on ___' box to the ICU daily ward-round template that becomes mandatory on day 3.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive at-risk admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU MDT governance. If it works, add the goals to the ICU discharge summary so they travel to the ward.
evidence: [1827] Cork older-person rehabilitation unit: goal setting 18% → 40%, SMART goals 4% → 28% (structured MDT booklet)
[2790] Morriston ICU: Clinical Frailty Scale completion 52% → 68% (posters, handover reminders)
pitfalls: Physiotherapists record goals in a separate system → agree before cycle 1 which records count.
Sedated patients cannot agree goals → count family involvement or documented reason, as NICE allows.
At-risk definition changes between cycles → write the criteria on the data sheet.
Weekend admissions missed → report weekday and weekend admissions separately.
pearls: Recruit the lead ICU physiotherapist as co-lead.
Use the NCEPOD 2025 audit toolkit fields where they match.
Present with a patient story from the follow-up clinic.
Add the box to the day-3 ward round so it is part of routine care.

question: In adults at risk of long-term problems who move from critical care to a general ward, what proportion have a written handover that includes their rehabilitation programme?
why: ICU discharge letters were poor in a UHBW audit [77] and handover information was often incomplete at the theatre–critical care interface [2271]; no audit in the library checks that rehabilitation plans reach the ward.

standard.source: NICE QS158 statement 2 (2017), from NICE CG83 rec 1.12 and CG50 rec 1.15
standard.wording: Adults at risk of morbidity have a formal handover of care, including their agreed individualised structured rehabilitation programme, when they transfer from critical care to a general ward.

pass: The ICU discharge summary or handover document contains the rehabilitation goals and the plan (therapy frequency, mobility level, referrals) for the ward team.
population: Adults discharged alive from ICU/HDU to a general ward who met an 'at risk' criterion during the stay. Exclude transfers to other hospitals and palliative discharges.
sample: 40 consecutive at-risk ward discharges over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ICU discharge summary and therapy handover notes in the EPR.

reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive at-risk discharges, same template.

[2271] Royal Papworth theatre-to-critical care handover: specific postoperative instructions 30% → 45%
[1827] Cork rehabilitation unit: goal setting 18% → 40% (structured booklet)

Summary written by a junior doctor without therapy input → build the section so the physiotherapist can complete it.
Night discharges skip the summary → cross-check with audit 'night discharges'.
Section filled with 'see physio notes' → define what counts as a plan.

Check 48-hour ward therapy review as an outcome; it shows impact.
Use the same at-risk list as the rehabilitation-goals audit.
Ask the EPR team for a template change early; it can take weeks.

question: In adults who stayed in critical care for more than 4 days and were at risk of long-term problems, what proportion are reviewed 2 to 3 months after critical care discharge?
why: NCEPOD's 2025 report 'Recovery beyond survival' found a lack of follow-up after intensive care. No audit of post-ICU follow-up is in the library.

standard.source: NICE QS158 statement 4 (2017), from NICE CG83 recs 1.1 and 1.23
standard.wording: Adults who stayed in critical care for more than 4 days and were at risk of morbidity have a review 2 to 3 months after discharge from critical care.

pass: A face-to-face or video review by a critical care follow-up service (or equivalent) between 8 and 13 weeks after ICU discharge.
population: Adults with an ICU/HDU stay over 4 days who were at risk of morbidity and survived to hospital discharge. Exclude patients transferred out of area and those who declined follow-up (record separately).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients discharged from ICU 3–6 months ago.
data_source: ICU admission system (length of stay, discharge date); outpatient booking system and follow-up clinic letters.

change: Make an automatic follow-up clinic referral from the ICU discharge form for every patient with a stay over 4 days, with an opt-out reason.
target: ≥75% of eligible patients reviewed at 2–3 months
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 audit referrals; full re-audit of attendance 3 months later with the same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU governance and to the commissioning lead. If it works, report follow-up rates on the ICU dashboard.

[77] UHBW ICU-to-ward transfers: poor discharge letters → discharge letter improved

Outcome lags by 3 months → audit referral rate at re-audit and attendance later.
Patients die or move after discharge → exclude and report them separately.
Clinic capacity fills → agree nurse-led or virtual review models with the ICU lead.

Ask ICUsteps or the patient group for a patient voice at the presentation.
The NCEPOD 2025 audit toolkit fits this audit.
Separate 'not offered' from 'did not attend'.

question: In adults who had a critical care stay and received rehabilitation on the ward, what proportion are given their own copy of the critical care discharge summary before leaving hospital?

question: At pre-operative assessment, what proportion of adults aged over 80 or with diabetes have a lying-to-standing or sitting-to-standing blood pressure recorded?
why: Postural hypotension raises the risk of postoperative falls and longer stay. The 2026 guideline added postural screening; no library audit has measured it, and intra-operative hypotension audits show the gap [1935].

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026), recommendation 6
standard.wording: Patients at risk of postural hypotension including those who are symptomatic, aged > 80 y or who are diabetic, should be screened with a supine-to-stand blood pressure assessment or a sit-to-stand assessment (if more pragmatic).

pass: A lying (or sitting) and standing blood pressure pair documented at the pre-assessment visit, with action recorded if the drop is ≥20/10 mmHg.
population: Adults aged over 80, or with diabetes, or with postural symptoms, attending nurse-led or anaesthetist pre-assessment for elective surgery. Exclude patients who cannot stand.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible pre-assessment attendances over 2 weeks.
data_source: Pre-assessment record (observations, history); electronic pre-op assessment system.

Automated cuffs give wrong readings on standing → agree a method (1 and 3 minutes) before cycle 1.

Ask the falls team to support the presentation.
Report the number of significant drops found; it motivates staff.
Use the same eligibility list in both cycles.

question: Of elective operations cancelled on the day for high blood pressure, what proportion had a blood pressure below 180/120 mmHg?
why: Day-of-surgery cancellations waste theatre time; the 2026 guideline states surgery should proceed below stage 3 hypertension. Library cancellation audits focus on fasting and fitness [2193] [2748], not blood pressure thresholds.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026)
standard.wording: A blood pressure measurement should be performed in the pre-operative clinic using best practice as outlined in this guideline. Surgery should proceed unless the blood pressure is ≥ 180/120 (stage 3 hypertension).

sample: All such cancellations over the last 12 months (expect 20–50 in a DGH).
